blocks.source: Source: MLS® data from the Greater Vancouver REALTORS® and the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, compiled by SnapStats®. Sales ratio is homes sold divided by homes listed. On the reports’ own scale under 12% is a buyers’ market, 12% to 20% is balanced and over 20% is a sellers’ market. With fewer than ten homes listed, one sale moves the ratio a long way, so treat it as a rough signal.

blocks.text: Looking across the period, Detached houses: 35 sold over 5 months against an average of 58.6 listed, about 8.4 months of listings at that pace; the busiest month was October with 12 sold. Condos and townhomes: 18 sold over 5 months against an average of 17.6 listed, about 4.9 months of listings at that pace; the busiest month was June with 5 sold.

The City publishes no boundary for the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) sub-area as such, so any Albion boundary is not verified as an official line; the Albion Area Plan's Schedule 1 map is the closest official boundary document, and this page's working scope is the residential corridors on 240 Street, 102 Avenue and 104 Avenue, the Albion Fairgrounds and Sports Complex lands by the Fraser River, and farmland in South Albion.
Albion sits next to Cottonwood and East Central to the west along Lougheed Highway, Thornhill to the northeast, Kanaka Creek ground to the north, and the Fraser River along its south edge.

Albion's planned stock is a mix of house forms set by its own Area Plan, not a single house type: the plan's residential designations are Low Density Residential (single detached at an urban standard), Ground-Oriented Residential, Cluster Residential and Townhouse, plus an Albion Village Commercial node.

The growth pattern behind the newer houses here is the Area Plan itself: Council's October 28, 2025 update supports growth of local commercial nodes and adds buffers where urban development meets farmland, across a range of housing styles.

South Albion lots meet farmland: the 2025 plan update introduces buffers where urban development meets farmland, and Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR) status is a per-parcel check on the Agricultural Land Commission's mapping.

blocks.text: Albion: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The Albion Fairgrounds hosts events year-round, including Country Fest, the Caribbean Festival and the Home Show, and the Albion Sport Complex beside it is home to Planet Ice (ice rink) and the Golden Ears Winter Club (curling) — event-day traffic on the surrounding streets is part of living here.
Kanaka Creek Regional Park (Metro Vancouver) runs along Albion's west side, with the Canyon Trail to Cliff Falls and the Bell-Irving Hatchery.
No library branch sits in Albion; the Maple Ridge Public Library (Fraser Valley Regional Library) is at 130 – 22470 Dewdney Trunk Road in the Town Centre.
School District No. 42 has no middle tier: elementary schools are Kindergarten to Grade 7 and secondary schools are Grades 8 to 12, so Albion children change schools after Grade 7.

Albion Area Plan update, City of Maple Ridge: Council adopted updates on October 28, 2025, covering walking and cycling connections, local commercial nodes and farmland buffers. STATUS: adopted; read 2026-11-03.

Langley–Haney Place Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), TransLink: 22 kilometres between Willowbrook and Haney Place with peak service every 10 minutes, in detailed planning; designs, costs and timelines are not yet determined, and the route serves Albion via Haney Place to the west. STATUS: detailed planning; read 2026-11-03.
Lougheed Highway (Highway 7) runs along Albion's south side and 240 Street is its main north–south road, with 102 Avenue and 104 Avenue running east–west through the residential area.
Haney Place Exchange, in the Town Centre to the west, is the bus hub for this side of the city; the R3 Lougheed Hwy RapidBus runs from Coquitlam Central Station to Haney Place.

West Coast Express trains run weekdays between Waterfront Station (downtown Vancouver) and Mission City, with Port Haney Station at 22300 River Road and Maple Meadows Station at 20010 Dunn Avenue serving the west side of the city — no station sits in Albion.

Check floodplain status lot by lot on the south edge: the City's floodplain construction document sets the 6.7-metre flood construction level, a covenant on title identifies construction in the floodplain, and which Albion lots are affected is per-parcel only.
Check Agricultural Land Reserve status lot by lot in South Albion on the Agricultural Land Commission's mapping before assuming a house lot can be subdivided, filled or given a second dwelling.

Check the Albion Area Plan Schedule 1 designation for any lot near 248 Street or a commercial node: plan designations here were updated October 28, 2025, and a lot's designation, not its current house, decides what can be built next.

faq.q: Is Albion an official neighbourhood or just a listing label?
faq.a: It is both, which is unusual in Maple Ridge. The City lists "Albion/Kanaka" among its neighbourhoods, the Official Community Plan carries an Albion Area Plan for the same ground, and the board uses "Albion" as the sub-area name — unlike West Central and East Central, which are board names only.

faq.q: What changed in the 2025 Albion Area Plan update?
faq.a: Council adopted the update on October 28, 2025. It enhances walking and cycling connections, supports growth of local commercial nodes, introduces buffers where urban development meets farmland, and balances new residential development against protection of environmentally sensitive areas.

Albion Elementary (10031 240 Street), c'usqunela Elementary (24093 104 Avenue) and Samuel Robertson Technical Secondary (10445 245 Street) are in the area, with Kanaka Creek Elementary (11120 234a Street) at its west edge — addresses per the BC Ministry K-12 school file; catchments are address-specific, so check any address in the SD42 School Locator.

faq.q: What did the 2025 Albion Area Plan update change?
faq.a: Council adopted the update on October 28, 2025: it enhances walking and cycling connections, supports growth of local commercial nodes, introduces buffers where urban development meets farmland, and consolidates land-use policies to reflect provincial housing legislation.
